# Programs, Processes and the Kernel

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against man7.org `syscalls(2)`, `open(2)`, `fork(2)`, `waitpid(2)`, `signal(7)`, `pipe(7)`, `socket(2)`, `proc_pid_fd(5)`, `strace(1)`, `null(4)`; the GNU Bash manual (exit status); docs.python.org (`id()`); Kubernetes and Docker docs (exit code 137, `docker stop`); and *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces* chapters 4 and 6. All demos were re-run on macOS (Apple M4); the Linux commands were not run here.

Starts from: the CPU, RAM and disk picture from the previous lesson. Nothing else.

## The problem and why it matters

Production errors use this vocabulary: "Too many open files", "Permission denied", "exited with code 137", "segmentation fault", "Killed". If *process*, *kernel*, *system call* and *file descriptor* are fuzzy words, every log line is a guess. With them sharp, the same lines name their own cause.

## First principles

1. **A program is a file. A process is that program running.** The program is instructions sitting on disk. A *process* is what the operating system builds when you run it: its own private memory, a number that identifies it (the *process ID*, or *pid*), a list of open files, and at least one *thread* (one stream of instructions the CPU can run). Run one program twice and you get two processes.
2. **The kernel is the one piece of software in charge of the machine.** People say *operating system* (OS) to mean the kernel plus the tools around it (shell, `ps`, libraries). The kernel alone drives the hardware: it decides which thread gets which CPU core, hands out memory, and talks to disks and network cards.
3. **Your code runs with restricted rights; the kernel does not.** CPUs have a privileged mode and an unprivileged one. Ordinary programs run unprivileged (called *user space*) and cannot touch hardware or another process's memory. The kernel runs privileged (*kernel space*). This is what stops one buggy program from corrupting the rest.
4. **A system call is the only way across that wall.** It is a request from a process to the kernel: open a file, send bytes, start a process, get more memory. Linux's own manual calls it "the fundamental interface between an application and the Linux kernel", and notes that programs usually reach it through small wrapper functions in the C library. Because the CPU must switch into privileged mode and back, a system call costs more than an ordinary function call. How much more is something to measure, not recall.
5. **A file descriptor is a small integer that names something you opened.** The kernel keeps a per-process table; `open` returns "the lowest-numbered file descriptor not currently open for the process". It might point at a file, a pipe (a one-way byte channel between two processes), a network socket (one end of a network connection), or a terminal. By convention 0 is *standard input*, 1 is *standard output*, 2 is *standard error*. The table has a size limit.
6. **Processes are created by copying, and end with a status.** `fork` makes a child that is a near-copy of the parent. The parent can wait for it and read its *exit status*. A process killed by a *signal* (a numbered notification the kernel can deliver to a process) reports that instead.

## How it works

### The wall between your code and the kernel

```
  user space (unprivileged)
  +----------+  +----------+  +----------+
  | process  |  | process  |  | process  |
  | pid 101  |  | pid 102  |  | pid 103  |
  +----+-----+  +----+-----+  +----+-----+
       |  system call (open, read, write, fork ...)
  =====v=============v=============v==========
  kernel space (privileged)
  scheduler | memory | files | network
  ===========================================
       |             |             |
     CPU           RAM      disk / network card
```

### A process's table of file descriptors

```
  process pid 101              kernel objects
  fd 0 -----------------------> terminal (input)
  fd 1 -----------------------> terminal (output)
  fd 2 -----------------------> terminal (errors)
  fd 3 -----------------------> /etc/hosts (file)
  fd 4 -----------------------> network connection
  fd 5 -----------------------> (free: next open gets 5)
```

### Demo 1: processes, parents and pids

```bash
sleep 60 & P1=$!; sleep 60 & P2=$!
ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p $P1,$P2; kill $P1 $P2
```

Captured here on macOS (pids will differ; Linux `ps` takes the same flags):

```text
  PID  PPID COMM
78054 78053 sleep
78055 78053 sleep
```

One program (`/bin/sleep`), two processes, two pids, same parent (my shell). Every process has a parent (`PPID`); following parents leads back to pid 1, which is `launchd` on this Mac and shows `PPID` 0 (`ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p 1`; Linux not run).

### Demo 2: a copy has its own memory, and crashes stay inside

```python
import os
counter = [0]
pid = os.fork()                       # the kernel makes a near-copy of this process
if pid == 0:                          # in the child, fork() returned 0
    counter[0] = 99
    print(f"child  pid={os.getpid()} parent={os.getppid()} "
          f"counter={counter[0]} addr={id(counter):#x}", flush=True)
    os._exit(0)
os.waitpid(pid, 0)
print(f"parent pid={os.getpid()} child={pid} "
      f"counter={counter[0]} addr={id(counter):#x}", flush=True)
```

Captured here on macOS (`fork` is Unix-only; `id()` is the object's memory address in CPython):

```text
child  pid=77272 parent=77264 counter=99 addr=0x1046cd780
parent pid=77264 child=77272 counter=0 addr=0x1046cd780
```

Same address, different values: each process has its own private view of memory (the Memory lesson explains how). Now make the child die from a crash signal on purpose:

```python
import os, signal
pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
    os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGSEGV)   # child crashes itself
_, status = os.waitpid(pid, 0)
print("child killed by signal:", os.WTERMSIG(status))
print("parent still alive, pid", os.getpid())
```

```text
child killed by signal: 11
parent still alive, pid 77274
```

Signal 11 is `SIGSEGV`, "Invalid memory reference" in `signal(7)`, the signal the kernel delivers when a process touches memory it may not. Here the child sent it to itself with `os.kill`, so no bad access happened, but the effect is the same one: the default action ends only that process. Shells report death-by-signal as 128 plus the signal number: after `kill` on a background `sleep`, the shell's status (`wait`/`$?`) was `143`, which is 128 + 15 (`SIGTERM`, the polite "please stop"). Exit code 137 is 128 + 9: `SIGKILL`, which cannot be caught or ignored.

### Demo 3: file descriptors

```python
import os, subprocess
f = open("/etc/hosts");  g = open("/etc/hosts")
print("fds:", f.fileno(), g.fileno())
print(subprocess.run(["lsof", "-p", str(os.getpid()), "-a", "-d", "3,4"],
                     capture_output=True, text=True).stdout)
```

Captured here on macOS (`lsof` exists on Linux too; there you can also `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd`, not run here):

```text
fds: 3 4
COMMAND   PID      USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF     NODE NAME
Python  76240 ryanhamby    3r   REG   1,17      213 53513122 /private/etc/hosts
Python  76240 ryanhamby    4r   REG   1,17      213 53513122 /private/etc/hosts
```

Lowest free numbers, 3 then 4, because 0-2 are taken. Now leak them on purpose with a small limit:

```bash
( ulimit -n 64; python3 -c '
files = []
try:
    while True: files.append(open("/etc/hosts"))
except OSError as e: print("failed after", len(files), "opens:", e)' )
```

```text
failed after 61 opens: [Errno 24] Too many open files: '/etc/hosts'
```

### Demo 4: system calls cost something

Two loops of 2 million iterations: one does Python arithmetic; the other writes one byte per iteration to `/dev/null` (a file that discards everything), one system call each.

```python
# nosys.py: stays in user space
x = 0
for _ in range(2_000_000):
    x += 1
```

```python
# syscalls.py: one system call per iteration
import os
fd = os.open("/dev/null", os.O_WRONLY)
for _ in range(2_000_000):
    os.write(fd, b"x")
```

Run each as `/usr/bin/time -p python3 FILE`.

Captured here on macOS:

```text
nosys:    real 0.08  user 0.07  sys 0.00
syscalls: real 0.82  user 0.23  sys 0.58
```

`user` is time spent running your own code in user mode; `sys` is time the kernel spent "on behalf of the process" (`getrusage`). The second loop is about ten times slower overall and most of the extra time shows up as `sys`. The ratio is this machine's; Python adds overhead to both loops.

To watch the calls themselves: on Linux, `strace -c python3 script.py` counts time, calls and errors for each system call (not run here). macOS's `dtruss` is the nearest tool; it is installed here but I did not run it.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a service runs fine for hours, then every request fails with `Too many open files`. A restart cures it for a few hours.

1. **Count the descriptors.** `lsof -p <pid> | wc -l` (or `ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l` on Linux) climbs steadily while traffic is flat. That is a leak, not load.
2. **Name what is leaking.** In the `TYPE` column of `lsof`, are they sockets, files, or pipes? Sockets to one destination point at connections that are opened per request and never closed.
3. **Find the code path.** Look for an `open` or connect with no matching close on an error path. Wrap in `with` or `try/finally`.
4. **Check the limit.** `ulimit -n` shows the per-process cap. Raising it is a legitimate safety margin, but it only delays a leak.

**Fix:** close descriptors on every path, add a gauge of open descriptors to your metrics, and alert on its growth rate rather than waiting for the limit.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Separate processes: you want isolation (a crash or leak stays contained) and independent restarts | You need to share large data constantly; copying between processes is costly |
| Many small system calls are acceptable at low rates | A hot loop makes one system call per byte; batch the work |
| Raising `ulimit -n` as a margin | Raising it as the fix for a leak |

## Interview questions

1. What is the difference between a program and a process? *Probe:* two copies of one program? *Outline:* file vs running instance; two pids, separate memory.
2. What is the kernel, and why do user programs not simply talk to the hardware? *Outline:* privileged mode; isolation; the kernel arbitrates shared hardware.
3. What is a system call and why is it not free? *Outline:* the request crosses into privileged mode and back; measure with `time`, see `sys`; batch work to make fewer calls.
4. What is a file descriptor? Why do sockets have them? *Outline:* per-process handle for files, pipes, sockets; same table, same limit.
5. A container exits with code 137. What does that tell you? *Outline:* 128 + 9, killed by `SIGKILL`; Kubernetes reports memory-limit kills as `OOMKilled` with exit code 137, and `docker stop` sends `SIGTERM` then, after a grace period, `SIGKILL`. Confirm from logs.
6. Why does one process crashing not take down its neighbours? *Outline:* separate address spaces; the kernel kills only the offender.

**Whiteboard exercise:** a web server accepts a connection, reads a file and sends it. Draw the process, its descriptor table (listener, client socket, file), and each system call crossing the wall, in order.

## Checklist

1. I can say what a program, process, thread, kernel and system call are.
2. I can explain fds 0, 1, 2 and why a leak ends in "Too many open files".
3. I can read exit codes 143 and 137 and the shell's 128-plus rule.
4. I ran the fork, `lsof` and user-versus-sys demos.
5. I know `strace` watches system calls on Linux (not run here).

## Common wrong answers

- "A process is a thread." A process contains threads and owns the memory and descriptors they share.
- "The OS is the GUI." It is the kernel plus tools; servers have no GUI.
- "Raising the open-files limit fixes the leak." It buys time.
- "Exit codes 1 and 137 mean the same." 1 is the program's choice; 137 conventionally means a signal (9) ended it.

## Sources

Checked:
- man7.org `syscalls(2)`: the "fundamental interface" quote; wrappers in glibc.
- man7.org `fork(2)`: child and parent run in separate memory spaces, copy-on-write on Linux, return values. The macOS `fork` page does not mention copy-on-write.
- man7.org `open(2)`: "lowest-numbered file descriptor not currently open"; `EMFILE`. `proc_pid_fd(5)`: `/proc/pid/fd` has one link per open descriptor, 0, 1, 2 are stdin, stdout, stderr. `pipe(7)`: "unidirectional interprocess communication channel". `socket(2)`: "an endpoint for communication".
- man7.org `signal(7)`: SIGSEGV 11 "Invalid memory reference", SIGTERM 15, SIGKILL 9 cannot be caught, blocked or ignored (numbers are for x86 and ARM; they vary on some architectures). `waitpid(2)`: `WIFSIGNALED`, `WTERMSIG`. GNU Bash manual: "128+N" exit status.
- `strace(1)` `-c`; `null(4)` ("data written ... is discarded"); macOS `getrusage` (`ru_utime`, `ru_stime`); Python docs `id()` ("the address of the object in memory" in CPython).
- Kubernetes "Assign Memory Resources" (`OOMKilled`, exit code 137); Docker `docker stop` (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period).
- *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces* chapter 4 (process, address space, open files, three default descriptors) and chapter 6 (user mode, kernel mode, system call, trap).
- Demos: all re-run on one Apple M4 Mac (macOS): `ps`, fork (same address, 99 and 0), signal 11, `lsof` (fds 3 and 4), 61 opens under `ulimit -n 64`, `$?` 143 and 137 from `kill` and `kill -9`, timing (`nosys` 0.07s, `syscalls` 0.82s with `sys` 0.58s).
- Not run: `/proc/<pid>/fd`, `strace`, and `dtruss` (installed here, not run).
